sections.h2: Why heat is an engineering problem, not a climate note
sections.html:
Every charger has a derating curve. The question a buyer should ask is not "what is the operating range" but at which ambient temperature does output start to fall, and by how much. A datasheet that gives a range without that breakpoint is a marketing document.

In the Middle East the breakpoint arrives during the busiest commercial hours. A unit that reduces output above 45°C has a different commercial profile from one that holds rated power — because utilization and revenue both peak in the afternoon, not at 03:00.

sections.h2: What the Israeli network runs on
sections.html:
Our largest DC charging station partner in Israel began deploying our equipment in 2025 and has since taken multiple batches of 120–180 kW multi-standard DC fast chargers. That is a repeat-procurement signal, not a one-off pilot: the units sit in public networks serving both private drivers and commercial fleets.

Multi-standard output matters in that market because the vehicle parc is mixed. A site that covers only one connector standard halves its addressable traffic — and in a hot climate, hardware that runs at part load for lack of compatible vehicles still pays the full thermal penalty.

deep_dives.summary: Deep dive: the thermal choices behind the numbers
deep_dives.html:
Three design decisions carry most of the hot-climate performance:

  • Thermal headroom above 45°C. Components and cooling paths are selected so the cabinet dissipates heat into already-hot ambient air without throttling the power stage.
  • Intelligent power distribution. Output moves between guns as sessions taper, so station-level utilization stays high rather than one cable idling at full allocation.
  • Industrial-grade components. Capacitors, fans and connectors rated for sustained high ambient rather than headline peak temperature.

The commercial consequence is straightforward: availability through July and August, when a hot-climate public network earns the bulk of its margin.

faq.q: Do DC fast chargers derate in extreme heat?
faq.a: Conventional units often do. Ours are designed with thermal headroom so rated output is held through prolonged ambient above 45°C, instead of reducing power during the hottest commercial hours.

faq.q: Which models were deployed in Israel and Saudi Arabia?
faq.a: Israel: 120–180 kW multi-standard DC fast chargers across multiple batches from 2025 onward. Saudi Arabia: 120 kW integrated floor-mounted DC fast chargers in a three-gun configuration.

faq.q: Why does a three-gun configuration matter in a hot climate?
faq.a: It serves more vehicles per grid connection. That raises revenue per available kilowatt and reduces the number of separate cabinets that each need thermal management in the same heat.

hot-climate.cta_p: Tell us your site's design ambient temperature and duty cycle, and we will come back with a configuration drawn from deployments that already run in that climate.

sections.h2: The cabinet decides winter uptime, not the cable
sections.html:
Operators tend to specify the vehicle side first — connector type, cable length, gun count. In a cold market that is the wrong order. The failure modes that matter happen inside the cabinet, and they are thermal and electrical.

  • Cold-start output. A charger rated to −30°C tells you nothing unless it states where output starts to fall. The requirement is: starts at −30°C and holds rated output through the cold end.
  • Cooling that still works. Forced air with sealed electronics avoids the fluid, pumps and seals a liquid loop introduces — maintenance items a parking operator does not want in a freezing climate.
  • Enclosure durability. IP54 with IK08 rating, because in parking structures vehicle contact is normal, not exceptional.
  • Input tolerance. Distribution networks dimensioned for buildings, not for 120 kW loads appearing unpredictably. Voltage-dip tripping in a parking business is pure cost with no revenue offset.

sections.h2: What the heater interface actually does
sections.html:
Our DC platform supports an optional heating module built for ultra-low-temperature sites. When activated, it rapidly raises the operating temperature of the critical power components so the charger reaches optimal output quickly instead of limping through a cold start.

The Georgian deployment uses 120 kW and 180 kW dual-gun integrated floor-mounted stations with that interface. The customer is the second charging network operator in Georgia to partner with us — relevant because a second operator buys after watching the first one's winter.

deep_dives.summary: Deep dive: the Kazakhstan arithmetic — twelve bays from one supply
deep_dives.html:
The operator's real question was not which charger to buy, but how much charging capacity could be added without a utility upgrade. That question has one answer in most Kazakh commercial locations, and it is not a large number.

Six dual-gun cabinets answer it: twelve service points from six supplies, with output allocated between bays by the cabinet rather than fixed per cable. Ordered in July 2026, in service in August 2026 — one month from purchase order to energisation.

The platform is rated −30 to +70°C with output reducing above 50°C, so the same hardware also covers July. That is the bonus the cold-climate buyer is really paying for: a charger specified for January that is not embarrassed in the summer.

faq.q: At what temperature does an EV charger start losing power?
faq.a: It depends on design. The Vulco platform is rated from −30 to +70°C with output reducing above 50°C, so rated output is held across the cold end rather than tapering in winter.

faq.q: Do electric buses and cars charge normally at minus 30°C?
faq.a: With the right cabinet, yes. The constraint is inside the charger: battery and electronics need to reach their operating window. Our optional heater module raises the temperature of critical power components so full output is available quickly after a cold start.

faq.q: Why forced-air cooling instead of liquid cooling in a freezing climate?
faq.a: A liquid loop handles sustained high ambient better, but in freezing conditions it adds fluid, pumps and seals that need trained maintenance. For a 120 kW parking application in Kazakhstan, sealed forced air is the lower-risk design.

cold-climate.cta_p: Send us your design winter temperature, grid capacity and dwell patterns — we will size the cabinet count and connector mix the way we did for these sites.

cards.html: A depot's load is spiky by design: most of the day a handful of buses charge, but before the morning and afternoon peaks a dozen need energy inside a narrow window, each with a published departure time.
Twelve dual-gun cabinets sharing output between bays, rather than 24 dedicated high-power bays that would require an unjustifiable grid connection.
Twenty-four service points from twelve supplies, energised in ten weeks, with a winter specification the timetable can rely on.

sections.h2: Three ways to handle a depot peak, and the two that fail
sections.html:
A bus depot is a factory with a timetable. Most charging projects are judged on energy delivered per day; a depot is judged on whether the vehicle scheduled to leave at 06:40 left at 06:40 with enough charge to complete its block.

Depot sizing approaches and what each produces. Source: Anari Energy delivery records.
ApproachWhat happens
Size for the averageCheapest on paper. Produces a site that fails precisely when it is needed, because average demand is not what a depot presents at 05:30.
Size for the peak without sharingTechnically correct, commercially difficult. Two dozen dedicated high-power bays means a grid connection the operator cannot justify for the other twenty hours of the day.
Size for the peak with sharingWhat was built: fewer cabinets, more connectors, output allocated by the cabinet rather than fixed by the cable.

There is a fourth constraint that never appears in a tender document but always appears in the operating budget: at a bus depot a failed charge is not a lost fuel margin, it is a cancelled service and a passenger complaint. Depot downtime costs an order of magnitude more than downtime at a retail charger.

Each cabinet serves two vehicles and allocates output between them. Where one bus needs the full rate it takes all 120 kW; where two dwell together the cabinet splits. Twenty-four service points from twelve supplies is the arithmetic that makes the site viable, and allocation follows the schedule rather than a fixed bay assignment.

Higher power would have bought speed the timetable cannot use, at a connection cost the site would have to fund. A bus that returns at 30% state of charge and departs four hours later does not need the fastest possible charge — it needs enough energy inside its dwell window at a price the timetable can carry.

sections.h2: Why the specification matters in February
sections.html: The Vulco platform is rated from −30 to +70°C, with output reducing above 50°C. A depot that cannot charge in February does not have a slow site; it has a schedule failure. Cold-end rated output is therefore a timetable requirement rather than a comfort spec.

deep_dives.summary: Deep dive: the ten weeks between order and power-on
deep_dives.html:
Ordered in May 2026, energised in July 2026. For a 24-bay depot that timeline is a product of what does not have to happen: no new substation, no enlarged connection, no civil work to lay out two dozen dedicated high-power feeds.

What has to earn its keep afterwards is utilization. A shared-output depot charges at a lower per-bay peak and a higher per-site duty cycle — which is the profile a fixed timetable actually presents. The site is a bus station serving scheduled services, run by a commercial operator, and it sits inside the 100+ customers in 22 countries we have delivered to since 2021.

faq.q: How many chargers does a bus depot need?
faq.a: Start from the departure timetable, not from a nameplate target. This depot needed 24 service points but only 12 grid supplies: twelve dual-gun 120 kW cabinets, with output shared between bays to clear the peak.

faq.q: Can a depot avoid a utility upgrade?
faq.a: Usually yes, by sharing output across more connectors instead of installing one dedicated high-power bay per vehicle. That trades a marginal charging speed for a connection the operator can actually obtain.

faq.q: What happens to charging in winter at a bus depot?
faq.a: Depot winter performance is a schedule requirement. The platform is rated −30 to +70°C, so rated output is available at the cold end — a failed charge in February is a cancelled service, not a lost margin.

bus-depot-czechia.cta_p: Send us your departure schedule and available grid capacity. We will size cabinet count and connector mix from the schedule backwards, the way this depot was built.

sections.h2: Why 22 kW AC is not a downgrade where DC is overkill
sections.html:
DC wins headlines; AC wins sites. Where a vehicle is parked for one to four hours, 22 kW delivers more energy per euro of installed capacity than a 120 kW cabinet the driver cannot use, because the car is leaving before the session finishes anyway.

The commercial logic is the grid connection. A fleet of 22 kW units can be added to an existing supply in stages; a single high-power DC cabinet often cannot be added at all without a distribution upgrade. That is why these deployments look small individually and are viable collectively.

sections.h2: The pattern behind the five sites
sections.html:
None of these sites was won on peak power. Each was won on a constraint the operator could not solve with a bigger cabinet:

  • Oman — corridors needed coverage across distance; AC units let the operator place chargers where DC load could not be justified yet.
  • Cyprus and Peru — small markets where a reliable unit with a service path behind it beats a powerful unit with no spares.
  • Italy — a police station where the requirement was install-and-forget, not maximum throughput.
  • Türkiye — the differentiator was the localisation centre. In any market, the second question after cost is who fixes it.

deep_dives.summary: Deep dive: what the 22 kW platform actually is
deep_dives.html:
The unit shipped to these five markets is a 22 kW Type 2 floor-mounted public charging station — a pedestal-mounted AC charger using the Type 2 connector standard used across the Middle East, Europe, Türkiye and Latin America. Floor-mounted rather than wall-mounted matters at public sites: it does not depend on a building owner agreeing to put fixings into their wall, and it survives car-park traffic that a wall box does not.

All five deployments sit under Anari Energy's delivery to 100+ customers in 22 countries since 2021, with local support from offices in Shenzhen, Xi'an, Istanbul and Dubai.

faq.q: Where has Anari deployed 22 kW AC charging?
faq.a: Five markets so far: Oman (highway corridors), Cyprus (public parking), Italy (a police station), Peru (a public parking lot) and Türkiye (public site alongside a localisation centre). All use the 22 kW Type 2 floor-mounted public charging station.

faq.q: Is 22 kW AC enough compared with DC fast charging?
faq.a: It depends on dwell time. Where a vehicle parks for one to four hours, 22 kW delivers more usable energy per euro of installed capacity, and it can often be added to an existing supply without a distribution upgrade.

faq.q: Why does a localisation centre matter for a charging project?
faq.a: Because the second question a buyer asks after price is who fixes it. A localisation centre holds spares, delivers service and configures product for the local market — which is what turns a one-off shipment into a supported installation.

sections.h2: Why the parking area is the right place for the panels
sections.html:
A car park is a large, flat, unshaded surface that already carries structure — which makes it the cheapest place on most industrial sites to put PV. Panels above the bays turn one asset into two: generation and shade. Vehicles park under it, the site generates under the same footprint, and no additional land is consumed.

The alternative most sites take is a PV field elsewhere on the site plus charging equipment near the building. That works, but generation and load end up coupled through a longer electrical path and two separate control philosophies.

sections.h2: The design decision that makes or breaks off-grid
sections.html:
Off-grid is not a hardware choice; it is an energy-balance choice. The system has to be sized against a consumption profile it cannot fully predict: how many vehicles, how much sun, how much storage, and what happens in a low-irradiance week.

  • Sizing the array against charging demand, not against the roof area available.
  • Sizing storage against the evening peak, when solar is gone but vehicles are still there.
  • Deciding which load is deferred when generation lags — EV charging is a flexible load, which is exactly why it pairs well with on-site generation.

That is why the deployment was designed as one system. Bought separately, each supplier optimises its own component and the site inherits the seams.

deep_dives.summary: Deep dive: what energy independence means commercially
deep_dives.html:
An industrial park that generates, stores and consumes on the same site is not only reducing carbon. It is converting an operating cost into a capital asset and reducing exposure to a grid connection it may not be able to expand.

For the park operator the visible benefit is charging availability; the structural benefit is that added charging capacity does not automatically mean an added utility application. The same logic applies where a grid upgrade is slow, expensive or simply not granted — often the binding constraint in emerging markets.

See the related PV + ESS + charging solution for how the three subsystems are scoped together.

faq.a: Photovoltaic generation, battery energy storage and EV charging designed as one system: the array generates, storage buffers, and charging consumes — with the goal of using on-site renewable energy instead of grid power.
Yes, if array, storage and charging are sized together against the site's consumption profile. EV charging is a flexible load, which makes it a good match for on-site generation and storage.

faq.q: Why put solar panels above a parking area?
faq.a: A car park is large, flat and already has structure. Panels above the bays generate electricity and shade vehicles in the same footprint, without consuming additional land.

cards.html: In a mature market you compete for share. Here the question is different: where does the first fast-charging capacity come from, and who can operate it.

Deployment shaped by the binding constraint at each site: maximum output where there is no network, right-sized distribution where the grid is the limit, mixed power where one site serves mixed vehicles.
Three sites that work with the constraint instead of against it — and a repeatable answer for markets where infrastructure arrives before demand.

sections.h2: Ethiopia: a policy that closed the door on combustion imports
sections.html:
Ethiopia's import restriction on internal combustion vehicles is the most aggressive electrification policy any government has enacted — introduced in 2024 and extended in 2025. The logic is energy economics: the country generates the overwhelming majority of its electricity from hydro and spends scarce foreign currency on imported fuel.

That reasoning is sound at the level of a ministry. At the level of a driver it creates an immediate problem: vehicles are arriving and the places to charge them are not. As of April 2025, Addis Ababa had two operational ultra-fast charging stations serving a national fleet being forced to electrify by policy.

For an operator, that map is the entire commercial thesis. In a mature market you compete for share against a dozen networks. Here you build the only place a vehicle can charge at speed on a given corridor. The site we commissioned runs 3 dual-gun 180 kW chargers — 6 connectors, 540 kW installed.

The obvious configuration for a commercial car park is one large cabinet. A Bulgarian parking operator ordered four Castor cabinets instead — two single-gun 20 kW and two dual-gun 30–40 kW — for six DC connectors at 120 kW total. Ordered September 2026, commissioned October 2026.

One 120 kW dual-gun cabinet would have carried the same headline number and delivered two connectors. The distributed layout won on three points:

  • Existing capacity. A city car park's supply is sized for lighting, lifts and HVAC. Four smaller feeds fit; one 120 kW load may trigger a distribution upgrade with a fee and a timeline the operator does not control.
  • Redundancy. A single cabinet is a single point of failure for the whole site. Four cabinets mean a fault removes one or two connectors and leaves the car park earning.
  • Habit, not throughput. Corridor charging is built by regulation and serves drivers passing through. A car park serves the driver already parked, where the goal is a charging habit among repeat visitors.

sections.h2: El Salvador: one site, two very different vehicles
sections.html:
The industrial facility needed charging for a delivery van and for something much larger at the same address. The answer was mixed power: a 40 kW dual-gun wallbox DC for the light end and a 180 kW three-gun integrated floor-mounted unit for heavy loads — both installed, commissioned and performance-tested before handover.

The deployment follows our entry into the Peruvian market and is part of a pattern across Latin America: sites that need a small amount of charging capability now, and a credible path to more later.

deep_dives.summary: Deep dive: what to buy when there is no market yet
deep_dives.html:
In a market without infrastructure the usual procurement logic inverts. Buyers are not optimising utilisation against a known fleet; they are placing a first asset on a corridor that will only become busy later.

Three rules fall out of the deployments on this page:

  • Where there is no network, output per site matters most — one 180 kW cabinet serving six vehicles does more for a market than four 22 kW units nobody drives to.
  • Where the grid is the limit, connectors beat kilowatts — distributed smaller cabinets on existing capacity open this year.
  • Where one site serves mixed vehicles, mixed power is cheaper than over-specifying everything — a 40 kW unit plus a 180 kW unit instead of two 180 kW units.

All of these sit inside the 100+ customers in 22 countries we have delivered to since 2021.

faq.q: What is the biggest constraint on EV charging in emerging markets?
faq.a: Grid capacity and service support, not charger technology. In Bulgaria the limit was the existing car-park supply; in Ethiopia it was the near-total absence of fast charging; in El Salvador it was one site serving vehicles of very different sizes.

faq.q: How much fast charging did Ethiopia have before this project?
faq.a: As of April 2025 the capital, Addis Ababa, had two operational ultra-fast charging stations capable of charging up to 32 vehicles simultaneously, for a national fleet being forced to electrify by an import restriction.

faq.q: Why install four smaller DC cabinets instead of one large one?
faq.a: Four smaller feeds can use an existing supply while a single large cabinet may require a distribution upgrade. A fault also takes out one or two connectors instead of the whole site.

emerging-markets.cta_h3: Building the first charging site in a market?
emerging-markets.cta_p: Tell us what grid capacity you can actually obtain and which vehicles will arrive first. We will size output and connector count to the constraint, not to a brochure.
